issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant is entitled to be released on bail.

facts: The appellant, accused of being a member of the Popular Front of India (PFI), was arrested on July 12, 2022.
He has been in custody for over two years and four months.
The chargesheet has been filed, but charges have not yet been framed.
The prosecution has cited 40 accused and 354 witnesses, indicating that the trial is not likely to conclude in the near future.
A co-accused with a similar role has already been granted bail by the Supreme Court.
law: Article 21 of the Constitution of India guarantees the right to life and personal liberty, which includes the right to a speedy trial.

Supreme Court precedents (such as Union of India v. K.A. Najeeb) establish that prolonged pre-trial detention without a reasonable prospect of the trial concluding soon violates Article 21 and can be a ground for granting bail.
application: The Court applied the principles of Article 21 to the facts of the case, noting the appellant's long period of incarceration (over two years and four months) without the trial even commencing.
It observed that with 40 accused and 354 witnesses, the trial is unlikely to be completed soon.
The Court reasoned that allowing the appellant to 'languish in jail indefinitely and that too without a trial' would be a clear violation of his fundamental rights under Article 21.
The Court also considered the principle of parity, as a co-accused in a similar position had already been granted bail.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant is entitled to be released on bail because his prolonged pre-trial detention, with no likelihood of a speedy trial, amounted to a violation of his fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution. The appeal was accordingly allowed.

cases.case_name: Union of India v. K.A. Najeeb
cases.principle: With the passage of time, the effect of strict statutory provisions for bail must be diluted to give way to the mandate of Part III of the Constitution. The constitutional right to a speedy trial will have precedence over the statutory bar, and the period of incarceration is a relevant factor for constitutional courts to consider, which cannot be solely governed by the statutory provisions.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Keeping the statutory provisions in mind but with the passage of time the effect of that statutory provision would in fact have to be diluted giving way to the mandate of Part III of the Constitution where the accused as of now is not a convict and is facing the charges. Constitutional right of speedy trial in such circumstances will have precedence over the bar/strict provisions of the statute and cannot be made the sole reason for denial of bail. Therefore, the period of incarceration of an accused could also be a relevant factor to be considered by the constitutional courts not to be merely governed by the statutory provisions.
